title: The Limits of High-Quality Curriculum Evaluation
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio responds to Natalie Wexler's dissection of the Benchmark Advance ELA curriculum by agreeing that knowledge-building curricula deserve careful scrutiny, then questioning whether such fine-grained evaluation matters when curriculum is not yet central to what students actually experience. He distinguishes curriculum as designed from curriculum as practiced, noting that teachers routinely adapt, supplement, skip and replace lessons and that reliance on outside resources is growing even as high-quality instructional materials spread. The hidden costs include enormous teacher time spent building lessons, which he recalls from his own early career. Citing David Steiner, he explains that avoidance often stems from teachers doubting students can manage grade-level rigor, which puts the onus on publishers and schools to supply diagnostics and interventions. His conclusion is that the intellectual argument for knowledge-rich curriculum has been largely won but the operational one has barely been attempted, and the central question is how to tell what students actually experience.
points: Evaluating the printed curriculum tells us little about the delivered one; it is like inferring children's diet by walking grocery aisles.
Customization is intensifying, not receding: teachers now draw on multiple programs and roughly five extra resources, so HQIM has been layered onto old habits rather than replacing them.
Pondiscio proposes reversing the default presumption, treating the curriculum as sound unless there is a clear evidence-based reason to depart from it.

quotes: To know whether a knowledge-building curriculum actually deserves that label, you have to look at what it asks students to do all day. Are students reading rich, content-heavy texts and grappling with ideas that build over time? Are lessons organized around coherent topics that accumulate knowledge, rather than disconnected skills practice? Do classroom tasks reflect what we know about how learning works—retrieval, attention to meaning, and sustained engagement with content—rather than superficial activities?

As students experience it” is the rub. It is more revealing to watch what people do than what they say. And what educators do with curriculum suggests that, for all our talk about its importance, it does not yet command real authority. It is still treated as optional—something to be reshaped or replaced at will—rather than the backbone of instruction.

A curriculum is a designed experience. It reflects deliberate decisions about what to teach, in what order, using which texts, and toward what ends. Done well, it reflects expertise and promotes coherence over time. But that is curriculum as design. Curriculum as practice in American schools is something else entirely.

Understand this is not an anomaly, it is our system. Teachers routinely adapt, supplement, skip, and replace lessons. This is not to suggest that teachers should simply “shut up and teach the script.” Thoughtful adaptation—grounded in evidence, aligned to the curriculum’s sequence, and responsive to student needs—is part of the craft.

The result is a wide and consequential gap between what is intended, what is implemented, and what students actually experience. And it is that last category—the experienced curriculum—that ultimately determines what students learn.

I spent 20 to 30 hours a week early in my career cobbling together lessons from scratch or searching for materials to “engage” students, differentiate instruction, or teach content-neutral “skills and strategies.” Those hours would have been far better spent studying student work, refining my delivery, or communicating with families.

We are observing what is printed, not what is delivered. It’s a bit like trying to infer children’s diet and nutrition by walking the aisles of a grocery store. The availability of healthy food is encouraging and tells you something about what is possible. It tells you very little about what children are actually eating.
